questions.q: The correct priority order for actions in an incident is:
options: Protect life, contain, inform & care, restore & record
questions.explain: P1 protect life, P2 contain, P3 inform & care, P4 restore & record. This order never changes, whatever the incident.

questions.q: P1 — 'Now' — class actions are those that:
options: Protect life: stop/protect movements, isolate energy, start rescue and first aid
questions.explain: P1 is only about life: protection, isolation, rescue. Everything else queues behind it.

questions.q: P2 — 'Next' — containment means:
options: Isolating the failed section or system so the problem cannot spread to healthy sections
questions.explain: Contain second: cut the failure off from the healthy railway so one problem cannot become five.

questions.q: P3 — 'Then' — covers:
options: Passengers informed and cared for — announcements, alternatives like bus bridging, agencies updated
questions.explain: After protection and containment comes people-care: honest information and practical alternatives.

questions.q: P4 — 'After' — includes:
options: Phased restoration of service, reporting, analysis and corrective action
questions.explain: Restore and record come last — phased resumption, then the report and analysis that prevent a repeat.

questions.q: The OODA loop used for decisions under time pressure stands for:
options: Observe, Orient, Decide, Act — then re-observe
questions.explain: Observe → Orient → Decide → Act → observe again. A decision is a loop, not a single event.

questions.q: In a time-critical situation, the controller should choose:
options: No option until the enquiry advises
The option that looks best in the report
The perfect option, however long it takes
The safest workable option available now, then revise as facts arrive
questions.explain: A good decision now beats a perfect decision late. Safety is never the thing traded away for speed or elegance.

questions.q: The 5 Whys technique works by:
options: Asking 'why' repeatedly until the answer reaches a fixable system cause
questions.explain: Each 'why' goes one layer deeper — past the person, to the system weakness that can actually be fixed.

questions.q: In 5 Whys analysis, a good stopping point is when:
options: The cause is a system weakness that can be fixed — e.g. two alarms sharing one tone, so the alarm was missed
A person has been named to blame
questions.explain: Stop at the system cause: 'the operator forgot' is not a root cause; 'the alarm was not distinctive' is fixable.

questions.q: The Fishbone (Ishikawa) diagram groups possible causes under:
questions.explain: The fishbone heads stop an enquiry from blaming the nearest human by forcing all cause families to be examined.

questions.q: Post-incident analysis begins with:
options: Reconstructing the timeline from logs, recordings and event data
questions.explain: Facts first: the timeline from logs and recordings is the skeleton on which all analysis hangs.

questions.q: The 'immediate cause' of an incident is:
options: What directly happened — the event that triggered the incident
questions.explain: Immediate cause = what happened. Underlying causes explain why it was possible; the root cause is the fixable system weakness.

questions.q: The 'root cause' differs from the immediate cause because it is:
options: The underlying system weakness whose correction prevents the whole class of incidents
questions.explain: Fixing the immediate cause repairs one incident. Fixing the root cause protects every future shift.

questions.q: A train fails in a section and passengers are waiting on two crowded platforms. The FIRST decision is:
options: Protect the section and the failed train, stopping/regulating other movements
questions.explain: Life and protection first (P1). Buses, announcements and analysis all follow in their P3/P4 order.

questions.q: Two trains are delayed and one spare train is available. The best prioritisation is to deploy the spare:
options: To the least crowded section to keep it simple
To the section nearest the depot
Where it restores headway for the maximum passengers on the worst-affected section
questions.explain: Scarce resources go where they do the most good — worst-affected section, maximum passengers, judged objectively.

questions.q: One platform line is free and two delayed trains need it. Allocation should be decided by:
options: Safety first, then passenger load and network impact
questions.explain: Objective criteria in safety order. Personal influence and noise are not prioritisation tools.

questions.q: A decision has been taken and new facts show it is no longer the best one. The controller should:
options: Change it openly and communicate the change to all concerned
Blame the junior who gave the facts
Stick to it to save face
questions.explain: Updating a decision on new facts is professionalism. The failure is hiding the change, not making it.

questions.q: After taking a major operational decision, the controller must:
options: Communicate it on the proper channel, monitor its effect, and record it
Wait for the next shift to check it
questions.explain: Decide → communicate → monitor → revise → record. An unmonitored decision is only half a decision.

questions.q: Why should a major decision and its reason be stated on the recorded channel?
options: So the reasoning is on record — the enquiry and the team can see what was decided, why, and on what facts
questions.explain: Recorded reasoning protects the decision-maker and lets the whole team act on the same understanding.

questions.q: A fire is reported on a train approaching a station, and simultaneously a minor signalling fault appears elsewhere. Correct prioritisation:
options: Wait to see which becomes bigger
Fix the signalling fault first — it is simpler
Fire first: protect life, bring the train to the station as per procedure; contain the minor fault in parallel/next
questions.explain: Risk ranks the work, not arrival order or simplicity. Life-safety is P1; the minor fault is contained next.

questions.q: An incident is unfolding and information is incomplete. Waiting for complete information before acting is wrong because:
options: Protection delayed is protection denied — the incident grows while you wait; act on the safest reading of available facts
questions.explain: Decide with 80% information, communicate, and revise. The clock does not stop for the incident — or for you.

questions.q: During an incident, 'safest containment' means:
options: The action that stops the situation getting worse with the least new risk — e.g. isolating the failed section
Closing the whole railway for the day
questions.explain: Containment first limits damage. Repair and restoration are later steps, in their own priority slots.

questions.q: A recurring signal failure at one location has caused three incidents this month. Analysis should focus on:
options: Which driver was present each time
The system pattern at that location — equipment, environment or method — through tools like 5 Whys and fishbone
questions.explain: Three incidents at one place are a system speaking. Analyse the pattern, not the people who happened to be there.

questions.q: Which sequence correctly shows immediate analysis during a live incident?
options: What failed → what it affects → what happens if nothing is done → safest containment
questions.explain: The four live questions keep the controller ahead of the incident instead of chasing it.

questions.q: A controller must choose between two workable options under time pressure, one safer but slower, one faster but riskier. The rule is:
options: Safety is never the trade — choose the safest workable option
questions.explain: Within time pressure, 'workable' means safe first. Speed is recovered later; an accident is not.

questions.q: Passenger information during a long incident is a P3 action. It should begin:
options: Early, alongside containment — people who are informed stay calmer and cooperate
questions.explain: Informing is care, and it starts early — not as an afterthought when the technical work is done.

questions.q: The purpose of timeline reconstruction after an incident is to:
options: Establish the true sequence of events from records, so causes can be separated from effects
questions.explain: Sequence reveals causation. Without a true timeline, analysis is opinion stacked on opinion.

questions.q: In fishbone analysis, a cause like 'the checklist step was badly worded' belongs under:
questions.explain: A badly worded checklist is a Method cause — the way of working, not the worker, was weak.

questions.q: A cause like 'the relay was life-expired' belongs under which fishbone head?
questions.explain: Equipment condition sits under Machine/Material. Grouping causes correctly keeps the analysis complete.

questions.q: Heavy fog on the day of an incident would be examined under which fishbone head?
questions.explain: Weather and surroundings are Environment causes — real contributors that no individual could control.

questions.q: A spare train, two buses and one engineering team are available for a major disruption. Prioritisation of these resources should be based on:
options: Equal shares to everyone regardless of need
Keeping resources in reserve for later
Safety needs first, then maximum passenger benefit and network recovery
questions.explain: Resources follow risk and benefit, not turn-taking. Hoarding help during an incident helps no one.

questions.q: After an incident, the analysis report should distinguish clearly between:
options: Immediate cause, underlying causes and root cause
questions.explain: Three levels of cause, three levels of fix. Mixing them produces weak corrective actions.

questions.q: A controller realises mid-incident that the situation is beyond his authority and resources. The correct decision-making step is:
options: Escalate immediately with a clear statement of the situation, actions taken and help needed
Hand over informally to a colleague
Wait for the shift to end
questions.explain: Recognising your limit and escalating early is itself a good decision. Late escalation is a common root cause.

questions.q: Why is 'who is to blame' the WRONG first question in incident analysis?
options: It stops people reporting honestly and hides the system causes — analysis must first establish what happened and why it was possible
questions.explain: Blame-first enquiries get silence and cover-ups. Fact-first analysis gets the system weakness that can actually be fixed.

questions.q: A decision taken under pressure turns out well. It should still be:
options: Recorded with its reasons, so the learning is available for training and future incidents
questions.explain: Good decisions are data too. Recording the reasoning turns one person's judgement into the whole team's learning.

questions.q: The Swiss-cheese model of accident causation teaches that an incident happens when:
options: The holes in several layers of defence — design, procedures, supervision, training — line up at the same moment, so no layer stops the event
questions.explain: No single layer is perfect; safety comes from layers covering each other's holes. Analysis therefore examines every layer, not just the last person's action.

questions.q: A month of delay data shows 5 locations causing most of the line's lost minutes, out of 40 stations. Applying the Pareto idea, analysis and resources should go first to:
options: Those few locations causing the bulk of the delays — fixing the vital few removes most of the loss
questions.explain: Pareto's pattern — a small share of causes producing most of the effect — is how limited engineering time is aimed. Equal effort everywhere is equal waste.

questions.q: Every time-critical decision has a 'decision deadline' — the last moment by which deciding still changes the outcome. A controller identifies it by asking:
options: 'What does the rule book's first page say?'
'After what point will my decision no longer be able to prevent the bad outcome?' — and decides before that point, with whatever information exists then
questions.explain: A perfect decision delivered after its deadline is worthless. Working backwards from the point of no return tells the controller how much thinking time he truly has.

questions.q: Between two possible actions in an incident, one is easily reversible (a train can be re-routed back) and the other is not (a section re-energised). Decision discipline says:
options: Take both at the same speed
The reversible action can be taken quickly on partial information; the irreversible one deserves the extra check, because it cannot be taken back
Always choose the irreversible one first
questions.explain: Reversibility buys speed: what can be undone can be tried. What cannot be undone — like restoring power — earns its pause for verification.

questions.q: A risk matrix helps prioritisation by placing each hazard according to:
options: How likely it is to happen (likelihood) combined with how bad it would be (severity) — high-likelihood, high-severity hazards get action first
questions.explain: Likelihood times severity is the common language of risk. It stops rare-but-deadly and frequent-but-small hazards from being treated as the same problem.
